Everyone understands that this opposing statement, first, depends on what it negates and, second, has a content just as concrete, intelligible, and “positive” as the first. In other words, it is something like A-B.
Otherwise there could be no argument. The person asserting A would not understand the person asserting B; there would be nothing to deny and nothing to answer.
Experience shows, however, that arguments are always possible.

And the same experience shows that when an argument actually takes place, its result is not usually the “victory” of one of the two participants. Instead, the argument produces a third assertion, C, in which both of the original assertions are present, though neither remains exactly as it was before the dispute.
In principle, then, one can always derive some new assertion by bringing together two assertions that exclude one another.
This is why every assertion can be called “synthetic”: it includes both an affirmative element and a negative element, each of which can also appear separately.

This example of discursive dialectic already allows us to grasp the meaning of two of the most important dialectical concepts, though their full meaning will become clear only in the Phenomenology itself—or, more precisely, in the System as a whole.
I mean the two concepts Hegel names with the ordinary German words Aufheben and Vermittlung.
The first, unfortunately, cannot really be translated by any single word. The second is extremely cumbersome in Russian.
The first word is almost made for dialectical use.
The verb aufheben means, first, “to destroy,” “abolish,” “revoke,” or “cancel”; second, “to preserve” or “keep”; and third, “to raise” or “lift up.”
The essence of dialectic can therefore be expressed by saying that it is the Aufhebung—the sublation—of a non-dialectical thing, existence, or being.
When a non-dialectical thing—a thing equal to itself, “identical” with itself—“becomes,” if we may put it this way, dialectical, it does three things at once.
First, it destroys, abolishes, cancels, or negates itself.
Second, through that very destruction it also preserves itself.
And third, by preserving itself through its own destruction, it raises itself “to a higher level,” acquiring a “higher” or more developed form of existence.
Since the identical entity from which the dialectical process begins is nothing other than the “thesis,” we can say that dialectic destroys the thesis while preserving it and, by doing so, raises it.
The thesis preserved in and through its own destruction—the thesis thus raised—is precisely the synthesis.

And since, as we have seen, every dialectical entity can be understood as a synthesis, we can say that dialectical being and dialectical existence are nothing other than an Aufhebung, a sublation: a self-cancellation that also preserves and raises what it cancels.

It is therefore precisely this self-destruction or self-cancellation that forms the source, nerve, or driving force of Aufhebung—that is, the very self-negation we previously called “negativity” when defining the antithesis.
From what has just been said, it is clear that the concept of Aufheben adds nothing fundamentally new to our understanding.
It is nevertheless extremely useful because it compresses into a single term the three fundamental dialectical categories of “identity,” “negativity,” and “totality.”

Unfortunately, Russian has no word that combines the three different meanings contained in the German Aufheben. I am therefore forced to use an artificial technical expression when translating Aufheben, Aufhebung, aufgehoben, and related forms: “dialectical sublimation,” “dialectically sublimated,” and so on.
We can therefore say that an entity is dialectical only because it has been “dialectically sublated,” and only insofar as it has been sublated in this way.
Without this sublation, it would remain eternally identical—unchangingly equal to itself—and would therefore not be dialectical at all.
But when it is dialectically sublated, three things happen.
First, in one sense it destroys itself, because it ceases to be only what it is and therefore also ceases to be non-dialectical, as it previously was.

Second, it nevertheless preserves itself in some way. It remains itself because its self-negation is its own: it is not something else that negates it, but it that negates itself—or, what comes to the same thing, it is negated by itself rather than by another.

Third, it remains itself despite its self-negation. By gathering this negation back into itself, it becomes larger and richer—if you like, “higher” and “better” than it was before its dialectical sublation.

We have already said enough about the “preserving” character of dialectical, that is, determinate, negation to see why the union of “cancellation” and “preservation” in the single concept of sublation should not trouble us.
But we should say something about the third meaning contained in it: “raising.”
By “raising” I mean everything that is ordinarily included in the idea of “progress.”
A being that “progresses” does not remain eternally and immutably equal to itself. It changes while nevertheless remaining itself.
And in changing, it becomes “higher,” “better,” “more developed,” “fuller,” “deeper,” and so on.
In every concrete case, the word “higher” means nothing more mysterious than this.
Yet all these meanings also share something that can be defined formally. This formal definition helps us understand what dialectical sublation means as a “raising.”
From a subjective and formal point of view, we can define dialectical “raising” as follows.

From the standpoint of the “raised” form of being or existence—that is, from the standpoint of the synthesis—we can understand and “derive” the forms that have not yet been raised, namely the thesis and antithesis.
The “raised” form is, so to speak, “higher” because from it one can “see more.”
From an objective and formal point of view, by contrast, we can say that what is “not yet raised” is a necessary but insufficient basis, or cause, of what is “raised.”
Clearly there could be nothing “raised” if there were nothing to raise.
But for something to become “raised,” it must also actually be raised. Something has to be introduced into it, some force has to be invested in it; something must, as it were, be added.
This is why what has been “raised” is, so to speak, “higher,” “better,” and so forth than what has not.
Once again, the example of discursive dialectic makes this clear.

When an argument—that is, a confrontation between opposed opinions, thesis and antithesis—produces a new opinion that unites them, this new opinion is, in principle, “higher” or “better” than either of the originals.
The person who holds one of the two opposed opinions does not know the opposing “antithetical” opinion, nor the “synthetic” opinion that brings them together. In that sense, he has no real choice.

But the person who knows the “result of the argument”—the result of this mutual testing of opposed opinions—knows not only both of the original positions but also something that is not fully contained in either.
He is therefore capable of making a conscious and well-grounded choice.

And if he chooses the synthetic opinion, he does so precisely because it is “better,” “broader,” “deeper,” and so on than the two original opinions—that is, than those that have not yet been dialectically sublated.
This example also shows that dialectical being, existence, or entity—that is, something dialectically sublated—is always a kind of result.
It does not simply drop ready-made from the sky. It always presupposes something.
It comes not “at the beginning” but “at the end.” It is not something “simple” but a “whole.” It is not merely something better made but something more complete.
So we can say that synthetic, sublated existence is higher than “thetic” existence precisely because it appears as a result.
In principle, a result is always better than its starting point.
Some effort was required to reach it, precisely because the starting point was not fully satisfactory.

Every result certainly contains what it came from. But in the result, this original starting point has been enriched or completed by the effort expended on it and has therefore become “richer,” “fuller,” “better”—in other words, “higher.”
To put it differently, dialectical being, existence, or entity is never merely a state or resting point within reality. It is also always a process, a kind of dialectical movement and development.

And because, through this development, the entity changes essentially while nevertheless remaining itself, we can define the dialectical process in purely formal terms as the entity’s becoming: its becoming-itself (Sichselbstwerden).
Unlike a non-dialectical thing, the dialectical entity does not simply be what it is. It becomes what it is through a process of development.
Its self-equality (Sichselbstgleichheit) is an equality in motion, and its unity is the unity of a process.
In our example, the synthetic opinion differs from the original thesis because it is generated by the process of argument and is nothing other than the result of that process.
And the fact that dialectical, or dialectically sublated, existence is always a certain dialectical movement or becoming is expressed in the concepts of Vermittlung and vermitteln.
Vermittlung means “mediation,” while vermitteln means “to mediate,” “to act as an intermediary.”
In dialectical usage, however, Vermittlung stands in contrast to Unmittelbarkeit, or “immediacy.”
Unmittelbar sein means to “be” or “exist immediately.” By contrast, vermittelt sein means to “be” or “exist”—if one may put it this way—mediately.

Russian cannot express this naturally, because the obvious word has a completely different meaning. We are therefore once again forced to invent artificial and rather cumbersome technical terms such as “mediation,” “to mediate,” “mediatedly,” and so on.
But the words themselves are not important. What matters is what they express or conceptualize.
And after everything we have said, the meaning should now be clear.
Let us return to our example of discourse.
The “thetic” opinion, the thesis, is stated completely immediately and without reference to any other opinion.
The “antithetical” opinion, the antithesis, is stated in relation to a thesis because it is directed precisely against that thesis.
Yet the antithesis too is immediate insofar as it does not contain the thesis—precisely because it negates it.
The “synthetic” opinion, by contrast, is connected both with the thesis and with the antithesis, and it is mediated by the latter.
The antithesis serves, as we say, as an “intermediary” between the synthesis and the thesis.
The synthesis differs from the thesis only because, so to speak, it sees the thesis through the antithesis, or “by means of” it.
It is “synthetic” because it has been sublated—that is, because it appears as the result of an argument.
And the “process” of the argument is nothing other than the intervention of the antithesis. The antithesis, so to speak, “persuades” the thesis to “become” a synthesis.
If you like, the antithesis is nothing other than the thesis’s becoming synthesis.
“Mediation,” then, is nothing other than the appearance or intervention of the antithesis—its activity and realization.
But the antithesis itself is nothing other than realized “negativity.”
So we can say that the source, nerve, or driving force of dialectic is “mediation.”
Only mediated being, existence, or entity is dialectical, because only mediated being includes “negativity.”
In other words, the dialectical entity is “mediated” by a kind of self-negation that preserves and raises what it negates.
And this means that a “mediated,” dialectical entity never exists merely in a “simple” way or merely “for others.” It also exists “for itself.”
To negate oneself consciously, after all, one must in some sense know oneself, be aware of oneself, understand oneself.
One must, so to speak, “reflect” oneself back into oneself, becoming one’s own reflection or “self-reflection” (die Reflexion in sich selbst).
The dialectical entity therefore exists and acts not “immediately” but reflectively, precisely because it is itself an “intermediary” between itself and its own existence.
This also means that its existence is conscious: it includes consciousness and experience of itself.
